messages.author: ac2d2e4dc0e3cb16
messages.subject: when is an expression evaluated in ggplot2 ?
parts:
I noticed the following, which I do not understand (ggplot2 0.9.3.1)
Try the following
a1<-factor(1:5)
ggplot()+geom_bar(aes(a1))->pic
print(pic)
a1<-factor(10:11)
print(pic)

I would expect that the second print gives the same result as the first print. pic is not changed after the first print. But it does nog give the same result.
It takes the second definition of a1(10:11) It appears that pic does not contain the value of the expression but the expression itself,
and that the expression is evaluated each time when printed.
This is not what I expected. If it is according spec, could anyone show it to me? And how could I avoid this?
Thanks
Frans

messages.author: 5a37f1244321fb07
messages.subject: RE: when is an expression evaluated in ggplot2 ?
parts:
Dear Frans,

If you write your code this way, the “pic” doesn’t change:

 

a1 <- data.frame(a1=factor(1:5))

 

pic <- ggplot(data=a1, aes(a1)) + geom_bar()

print(pic)

 

#change the data

a1 <- data.frame(a1=factor(10:11))

print(pic)

#same results as before

 

 

ggplot takes a data frame, where you used a vector in the layer call (geom_bar).

I am guessing ggplot is not actually mapping the data in your code….., so when you run “pic” (=R obeject which is “ggplot()+geom_bar(aes(a1))”), it will take a new data.

--Kaori

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: when is an expression evaluated in ggplot2 ?
parts:
> In my opinion it was very pleasant that in later versions of ggplot2 it was
> possible to use ggplot without specifying a dataframe. Am I correct that
> this is an (undocumented?) feature that should not be used?

You should _always_ use a data frame with ggplot2 - otherwise, as
you've noticed it will evaluate the variable in the global
environment, and this means that the plot may change even if the plot
specification does not. If it was possible for ggplot2 to never look
in the global environment, it would, but then functions you'd defined
there wouldn't work.

You may also finding looking at the output of aes(a1) to be informative.

Hadley
